item.text:
**Assessment**
Mixed, leaning negative. Jokowi’s 2024 record shows some real targeting of vulnerable people and households, especially in health access, social assistance targeting, and child re-entry to school. But the strongest rights and equality evidence cuts the other way: Papua abuses, discrimination against women and minorities, and only partial, uneven inclusion for disabled and marginalized communities.

**Claims**
- [Indonesia](https://www.who.int/about/accountability/results/who-results-report-2024-2025/country-profile/2024/indonesia) - World Health Organization, 2024. WHO says Indonesia reached 90% coverage, reduced out-of-pocket costs, and improved access to essential health services regardless of gender, age, or disability status. This supports priority for vulnerable groups in health access. IDs: `6B.3`, `6B.2`
- [Does Indonesia’s National Health Insurance Scheme mobile phone application, Mobile JKN, support health financing?](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240100893) - World Health Organization, 2024-12-06. WHO describes JKN as expanding access and financial protection, with Mobile JKN simplifying enrollment and payments for informal contributors. This is direct evidence of inclusion-oriented governance. IDs: `6B.3`, `6B.2`
- [BAPPENAS Perkuat Dukungan untuk Anak-Anak dan Keluarga Rentan](https://www.unicef.org/indonesia/id/press-releases/bappenas-perkuat-dukungan-untuk-anak-anak-dan-keluarga-rentan) - UNICEF Indonesia, 2024-04-25. Regsosek was presented as a tool to improve targeting and delivery of social assistance for poor and vulnerable households, including children and families hit by poverty or shocks. IDs: `6B.3`, `6B.2`
- [A Blueprint to Get Children Back to School in Indonesia](https://www.unicef.org/indonesia/stories/blueprint-get-children-back-school-indonesia) - UNICEF Indonesia, 2024-08-23. The government-led re-enrollment effort helped bring nearly 37,000 children back to learning and prevented about 149,000 from dropping out since 2021. That is strong evidence of prioritizing children, though millions remained out of school. IDs: `6B.3`, `6B.2`
- [Indonesia's Care Economy Report Launch Event](https://www.worldbank.org/en/events/2024/08/28/report-launch-event-the-care-economy-in-indonesia) - World Bank, 2024-08-28. The report framing says care investments are needed to improve women’s labor-force participation and the wellbeing of children and families, and that Indonesia adopted a care-economy roadmap. This supports a limited pro-women/pro-family policy orientation. IDs: `6B.3`
- [Indonesia Gender Equality Program](https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/indonesia/brief/gender-equality-for-growth-research-and-analytical-program-in-indonesia) - World Bank, accessed 2026. The program is aimed at closing gender gaps and promoting reforms and investments that expand women’s economic participation. This is positive evidence of attention to women, but it is programmatic rather than proof of broad realized protection. IDs: `6B.3`
- [Indonesia](https://data.unwomen.org/country/indonesia) - UN Women Data Hub, accessed 2026. The country profile shows persistent gender gaps, including low female parliamentary representation and continuing violence indicators, which cuts against any claim of comprehensive prioritization of women. IDs: `6B.3`
- [No Real Efforts to Address Discrimination, Abuses Against Marginalized Groups](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/01/11/indonesia-jokowis-term-ends-whimper-rights) - Human Rights Watch, 2024-01-11. HRW says Jokowi’s final year produced no major initiative to address discrimination against religious minorities, women, and LGBT people, and the new criminal code threatened speech and association. This is strong negative evidence. IDs: `6B.3`
- [Indonesia: Racism, Discrimination Against Indigenous Papuans](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/09/18/indonesia-racism-discrimination-against-indigenous-papuans) - Human Rights Watch, 2024-09-18. HRW says Indigenous Papuans faced arbitrary arrest, torture, extrajudicial killings, and forced displacement, with weak accountability. This is the clearest negative evidence against prioritizing a marginalized regional minority. IDs: `6B.3`
- [Indonesia’s Country Profile](https://www.who.int/about/accountability/results/who-results-report-2024-2025/country-profile/2024/indonesia) - World Health Organization, 2024. WHO’s equity framing includes disability status, which is positive for disabled access in health. But the evidence is still narrow to health and does not establish broad disability inclusion across society. IDs: `6B.3`
- [No Hijab Ban for Paskibraka Members on I-Day, Govt](https://en.antaranews.com/news/322483/no-hijab-ban-for-paskibraka-members-on-i-day-govt) - ANTARA News, 2024-08-14. The government corrected a discriminatory uniform practice by clarifying that female Muslim Paskibraka members could keep wearing hijabs. This is a narrow positive sign for women and religious identity. IDs: `6B.3`
- [Indonesia’s WASH Acts 2024](https://www.unicef.org/indonesia/id/wash/laporan/wash-acts-edisi-2024) - UNICEF Indonesia, 2025-04. Open defecation fell in 2024, but safely managed water and sanitation remained very low. This suggests limited but real attention to poor and remote communities, not full prioritization. IDs: `6B.3`, `6B.2`

**Search gap**
Direct 2024 evidence is strongest for children, women, Papua, and health access. It is much weaker for elderly people, disabled people beyond health coverage, and concrete poor-region outcomes outside Papua. Housing and food-security prioritization are also only indirectly evidenced through social-assistance and welfare targeting, not clean outcome data.
